# Results — Study 40 (Paper-Tiger): a published dual-momentum, mirrored back

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Monthly total-return prices for **SPY
(US), EFA (foreign), AGG (bonds)** plus the **^IRX 13-week T-bill** cash hurdle (Yahoo), 2003-09 →
2026-06. The strategy is Antonacci's **Global Equities Momentum** (relative momentum between US and
foreign equity, gated by an absolute-momentum T-bill filter into bonds), rebalanced monthly, **20 bp
per switch**. The offline core proves the machinery on a seeded synthetic world; this is the
measurement on the market. As-of **2026-06-30**; match the fingerprint below.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `REAL` · Tradability `FRAGILE` · "Beats the market"? `NOT SUPPORTED`

The vendor (paperswithbacktest, *"Momentum Asset Allocation"*, SSRN 1585517 = Antonacci) sells a
headline backtest and a Sharpe. Rebuilt faithfully on real ETFs, the strategy's signal **is real**:
net Sharpe **0.74** with a Lo (2002) t of **3.4** and a Newey-West HAC t of **3.6** — it makes money,
and the risk-adjusted return is statistically distinguishable from zero. But the *claim that sells it*
— that it beats buy-and-hold — is `NOT SUPPORTED`: its **0.74** ties plain SPY (**0.77**) and is
**beaten by a naïve 60/40 (0.86)**. What is real and valuable is one-dimensional: **crash protection**.
Its max drawdown is **−23%** against SPY's **−51%**, because the absolute-momentum filter sits in bonds
through 2008. That single dimension is `FRAGILE`: it rests on essentially **one** independent crisis in
the sample, it has **decayed since publication** (Sharpe 0.87 → 0.65), and as a portfolio sleeve it
**doesn't lift Sharpe at all** — it only trims drawdown. A real strategy; a paper-tiger headline.

## Data stamp

- **Universe**: SPY / EFA / AGG + ^IRX, 2003-09-30 → 2026-06-30, **261 invested months**, 35 switches,
  inputs fingerprint `e09091438e42`

## GEM vs the benchmarks that actually matter

| | Sharpe | CAGR | vol | max-DD | skew |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **GEM (net, 20 bp/switch)** | **0.74** | 8.9% | 12.5% | **−23%** | −0.39 |
| GEM (gross) | 0.77 | 9.2% | 12.5% | −23% | −0.39 |
| Buy & Hold SPY | 0.77 | 11.0% | 15.1% | −51% | −0.50 |
| 60/40 SPY/AGG (monthly rebalanced) | **0.86** | 8.0% | 9.6% | −32% | −0.55 |

On risk-adjusted return GEM does **not** beat just holding SPY, and it **loses to a plain 60/40**. The
"beats the market" headline is the paper tiger. (Note the vendor's own listed Sharpe for this idea is
`0.321` — *lower* than our 0.74; their figure is on a different universe/period. The point isn't that
their number is inflated, it's that **no** version of the number beats the right benchmark.)

## Is the signal real? Yes — the inference holds

- **Lo (2002)** annualised-Sharpe t-stat: **3.4** (Sharpe 0.74, n = 261 months).
- **Newey-West HAC** mean-return t-stat: **3.6** (mean +77 bp/month).

So `REAL` is earned — this is not a zero dressed up by a pretty equity curve. The teardown is about
*what kind* of real it is.

## What's actually real: crash protection (and only that)

| | GEM | SPY |
|---|---|---|
| mean return in the worst-decile SPY months (n = 27) | **−4.97%/mo** | −7.64%/mo |
| correlation to SPY *in those months* | **−0.01** | — |

In the months that hurt, GEM bleeds ~2.7 pts/month less than the index and is essentially uncorrelated
to it — the absolute-momentum filter is in bonds. That cushion is the entire edge.

## Why the cushion is `FRAGILE`, not `INVESTABLE`

1. **One crisis does the work.** Over 2003–2026 there is really one deep equity bear (2008) plus
   shallow ones (2020, 2022). The drawdown advantage is concentrated in a handful of months — a thin
   independent-observation count behind an impressive-looking 23-year chart.
2. **Post-publication decay.** Sub-period Sharpe: **2004–2013 0.87** → **2014–2026 0.65**. Antonacci
   published dual momentum in 2012–14; the edge is softer since (cf. McLean & Pontiff 2016).
3. **It doesn't improve a portfolio's Sharpe.** Blending a 30% GEM sleeve into a 60/40 leaves Sharpe
   at **0.86 → 0.86** while cutting max-DD **−32% → −27%**. Unlike a genuinely decorrelated sleeve
   (cf. study 31's trend book, which *raises* Sharpe), GEM only buys you a little less drawdown — and
   a 60/40 you already own gives more Sharpe for less effort.

## The honest takeaway

Dual momentum is a **real, sensible, low-turnover** crash-defensive rule — far from a mirage. But the
reason it *sells* (a backtest that "beats the market") does not survive a fair benchmark: it ties
buy-and-hold and loses to 60/40 on Sharpe, its one real gift (shallower drawdowns) leans on one crisis
and has faded since publication, and it adds no risk-adjusted return to a portfolio you'd plausibly
already hold. `REAL` signal, `FRAGILE` standalone, `NOT SUPPORTED` as a market-beater — which is a very
different study from the one the headline Sharpe advertises.
